readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: In Which None of the Characters Appear (Chapter I)
readings.challenge: Work out what is happening from sounds alone, as the dog outside the door must.
readings.focus: A mystery opening: a man writes something behind a closed door, rings, and leaves, and the only witness is a dog.
readings.context: Donald and Dorothy (1883) is by Mary Mapes Dodge, author of Hans Brinker and editor of St. Nicholas, a famous magazine for children. This very short first chapter is a puzzle that the rest of the book will explain, so read it twice. A quill pen is made from a feather; a bell-pull rang a bell in the servants’ part of the house; “at half-mast” means drooping, like a flag lowered halfway.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “In Which None of the Characters Appear,” the whole chapter; opens “The door of the study was closed, and only Nero was to be seen. He, poor dog, stood in…”; closes “…settled down on the rug before the study fire. For there was not a soul in the room.”.

questions.prompt: What does Nero hear through the door? List the sounds in order. What might the man be doing?
facilitatorNotes: Steps, a chair drawn to the table, rustling paper, a deep moan, a quill scratching fast, then silence. He seems to be writing something important and painful, perhaps a letter or a will; the moan suggests sorrow.
evidence: a deep-voiced moan; the rapid scratching of a quill pen

questions.prompt: How does the narrator show what Nero feels without the dog saying a word?
facilitatorNotes: His ears prick up, he droops “at half-mast,” his tail wags like a machine-crank meant to pull Liddy upstairs, he takes an “agonized glance,” and at last gives a deep sigh. Each movement shows a feeling.
evidence: poor Nero again stood at half-mast
as though it were the crank of some unseen machine

questions.prompt: The title says none of the characters appear, and the chapter ends, “For there was not a soul in the room.” Why might an author begin a book this way?
facilitatorNotes: To build a mystery: we do not know who the man is or what he wrote, and must wait to find out. The “dignified legs” are the only clue to who he is. Some readers will find this frustrating; others will want to read on.
evidence: For there was not a soul in the room.
a pair of dignified legs moving toward the great hall door

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: muffins and a puzzling uncle (Chapters V and VI, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice small signs that an adult is troubled, and keep track of them.
readings.focus: Uncle George begins an important talk, but keeps reacting strangely to Dorothy.
readings.context: Donald and Dorothy (1883) is by Mary Mapes Dodge, author of Hans Brinker and editor of St. Nicholas, a famous magazine for children. Fourteen-year-old twins Donald and Dorothy Reed (“the D’s”) live at Lakewood with their Uncle George. Their father died in England, and their mother was lost at sea when they were six weeks old; the babies were saved from the shipwreck by Jack, who now works for the family. Liddy (Lydia) is the housekeeper and Nero the old dog. That afternoon, on a drive, Dorothy saw a tall, thin stranger who has been hanging about the place. Trig means neat; perturbed means upset; a conference is a serious meeting; to domineer is to boss.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Supper-Time,” whole, and Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” through the twins’ exact age; opens “"OH, if gentlemen only knew the nature of muffins!"”; closes “"Yes, sir, right to a minute," replied Donald, laughing.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Liddy anxious at the start, and what does the joke about muffins show?
facilitatorNotes: Uncle George is late, and muffins must be eaten hot. The narrator makes fun of her worry, then lets her be satisfied: he does “appreciate the nature of muffins.” It is a light start before a serious talk.
evidence: if gentlemen only knew the nature of muffins
did appreciate the nature of muffins

questions.prompt: When Dorothy asks, “Did he know Aunt Kate?” how does everyone react, and what does that suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Donald looks frightened, Uncle George coughs, and Dorothy feels she can never mention her aunt “without raising a storm.” The subject is clearly painful for her uncle.
evidence: Donald looked frightened; Uncle George coughed
never to be able to speak of your own aunty without raising a storm

questions.prompt: Why does Uncle George suddenly pull his arm away and tell Dorothy to stop her nonsense? What does Donald think?
facilitatorNotes: Something in Dorothy’s manner upsets him, and Donald thinks “Uncle’s afraid again,” not angry. Readers may guess that she reminds him of someone, or that he is worried about something he has not said.
evidence: Now Uncle's afraid again
felt her uncle's arm immediately withdrawn

questions.prompt: Why is Dorothy glad that she and Donald are exactly the same age?
facilitatorNotes: Because neither twin can boss the other; they start “fair and square.” It shows how much she values being Donald’s equal.
evidence: twins can't boss--I mean domineer--each other

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: boarding school, a stranger and a tutor (Chapter VI, second part)
readings.challenge: Separate what Uncle George says from what he seems to be hiding.
readings.focus: Uncle George keeps Donald at home, warns the twins about a stranger, and tells them their tutor must leave.
readings.context: Recap: after supper Uncle George called the twins into the library for a serious talk, but kept stopping, and seemed troubled whenever Dorothy spoke of Aunt Kate. Apprehended here means feared; a ne’er-do-weel is a good-for-nothing; rudiments are first lessons; a tutor teaches children at home.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” from the talk of boarding-school to Uncle George’s plan to release Dr. Lane; opens “"Well, there is no hurry, I am glad to say. I have been thinking of late, Donald, that a…”; closes “…doctor the very next morning, if they would let him know when the lesson-hours were over.”.

questions.prompt: What does Donald imagine about boarding school, and what spoils the picture?
facilitatorNotes: A crack baseball club, a debating society, boxes of cake from home, even a fight or two; but he cannot imagine living without Dorry.
evidence: to get boxes of fruit and cake from home
but then how strange it would be to live without Dorry!

questions.prompt: Dorothy expects a warning about matches and bonfires. What is the warning really about, and what are the rules?
facilitatorNotes: The “long and lank” stranger. They must avoid him, never let him think they fear him, stay inside the gates and keep together.
evidence: Do not fear this man. Above all, do not let him imagine that you fear him.
Keep within the gates for the present.

questions.prompt: What does Uncle George tell the twins about the stranger, and what does he refuse to explain?
facilitatorNotes: He knew the man as a boy, and thinks he has been “going down for years.” He will not say why they must avoid him: “You need not see, nor try to see.” Readers may predict a link with the family’s past.
evidence: He is a ne'er-do-weel, whom I knew as a boy
You need not see, nor try to see.

questions.prompt: Dorothy cries “No more old algebra!” and then begs that Dr. Lane go at once. Is she selfish or kind? How does Donald know?
facilitatorNotes: Her first thought was a holiday, but she truly wants him to get well in the south, and Donald knows her well enough to see that she means it. A reader could call her both, one after the other.
evidence: Her vivid imagination had instantly pictured relief and a grand holiday.
She was thoroughly sincere and full of sympathy

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: Uncle George weeps (Chapter VI, third part)
readings.challenge: Listen to a character who says more than she meant to, and watch its effect.
readings.focus: Dorothy pours out her longing for a mother, and the twins learn what the shipwreck took from their uncle too.
readings.context: Recap: Uncle George has told the twins that Donald will not go to boarding school yet, warned them to avoid a stranger, and said their tutor must leave. Each time Dorothy mentioned Aunt Kate, he grew upset. A likeness is a portrait; impetuous means acting on sudden feeling; to reproach is to blame.
readings.contentNote: The family history is one of deaths: the twins’ father died in England, and their mother, aunt, uncle and baby cousin were lost at sea.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” from Donald’s question about boarding-school to Uncle George’s “Bless you, my little comforter”; opens “"Uncle!"”; closes “…my little comforter!--No. God be praised, we still have a great deal to be thankful for."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Dorothy say she has to ask about Aunt Kate? What is she really asking for?
facilitatorNotes: She is a girl with no mother and wants to know the women of her family; her mother’s portrait looks stiff to her, while Aunt Kate’s picture seems sweet and alive. She is asking for a mother’s story.
evidence: it's so hard, so awfully hard, to be a girl without any mother!
Aunt Kate's picture in the parlor is so different

questions.prompt: Dorothy starts to promise she will not be “so wicked again,” but stops. Why?
facilitatorNotes: She knows she has not been wicked, only quick to speak, so she will not say what is untrue even to apologise. She chooses a better word, “impetuous.”
evidence: She knew that she had not been wicked, and yet she could not at first hit upon the right term.

questions.prompt: What do the twins and their uncle say about the family’s past? Who was on the ship that went down?
facilitatorNotes: Their father died in England before he could sail. Their mother, Aunt Kate, Uncle Robertson and baby cousin Delia were all aboard, and the ship sank. Uncle George had hardly known the twins’ mother.
evidence: because he never lived to set sail from England
if the ship had landed safe

questions.prompt: How does Dorothy comfort her uncle, and does it work?
facilitatorNotes: She turns from what was lost to what they still have: the three of them together. He calls her his “little comforter” and gives thanks, so it does help.
evidence: It can't be so very miserable and dreadful with you and Donald and me left!
Bless you, my little comforter!

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: Jack the rescuer, and a man at the door (Chapter VI, end)
readings.challenge: Notice how characters tell a story they cannot really remember.
readings.focus: The twins retell their rescue at sea, then see the stranger outside at bedtime.
readings.context: Recap: in a tearful talk, Uncle George told the twins how much he had lost when their family’s ship went down, and Dorothy comforted him. A trump is a fine, dependable person; to capsize is to turn over; balusters are the posts of a stair rail; an edict is an order; remonstrances are protests.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A Family Conference,” from Donald’s mention of Liddy, Jack and Nero to the end of the chapter; opens “"Yes, and there are Liddy and Jack, and dear old Nero," said Donald, partly because he…”; closes “…minutes,--a great while for her,--thinking over the events of the day and evening.”.

questions.prompt: How can the twins describe the shipwreck when they were only six weeks old?
facilitatorNotes: They have talked about it so often that they feel they remember it; the narrator says so in brackets. Their argument about whether babies play pat-a-cake shows they are imagining.
evidence: The children had talked about the shipwreck so often that they felt as if they remembered the awful scene.
babies only six weeks old playing pat-a-cake! I guess not.

questions.prompt: What did Jack do to save them? Which act seems bravest to you?
facilitatorNotes: He caught the babies tossed from the ship, threw them into a boat, plunged back into the sea to save others, returned alone and half dead, and then cared for them until another ship picked them up. Readers may choose different acts.
evidence: plunging into the sea to save all he could, but able to get back alone, after all
wrapped us in blankets, and fed us

questions.prompt: The narrator says Dorothy’s joke about the rescue was in bad taste. Why does she make it anyway?
facilitatorNotes: She has had enough sad seriousness for one evening and jokes “in pure defiance” of it. Readers may sympathise with her need to lighten the mood, or agree with the narrator.
evidence: she had spoken in pure defiance of solemnity
There had been quite enough of that for one evening.

questions.prompt: Why did Donald open his window and cough? What does Dorothy’s goodnight show?
facilitatorNotes: He wanted his uncle to know he was near if there was trouble with the stranger. Dorothy teases “how good we are,” but kisses him soberly and lies awake: she is worried too.
evidence: You coughed, just to let Uncle know that you were around, if there should be any trouble.
but she kissed Donald soberly for good-night

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: ten Danbys from A to J (Chapter VII, first part)
readings.challenge: Keep track of a big cast by noticing what makes each person different.
readings.focus: The narrator introduces the poor, lively family next door, and Mrs. Danby talks and talks to Uncle George.
readings.context: Donald and Dorothy (1883) is by Mary Mapes Dodge, author of Hans Brinker and editor of St. Nicholas, a famous magazine for children. Fourteen-year-old twins Donald and Dorothy Reed (“the D’s”) live at Lakewood with their Uncle George. Their father died in England, and their mother was lost at sea when they were six weeks old; the babies were saved from the shipwreck by Jack, who now works for the family. Liddy (Lydia) is the housekeeper and Nero the old dog. Uncle George’s surname is Reed. A scow is a flat-bottomed boat; to parse a sentence is to name the part of speech of each word; deportment means behaviour; aspiration is hope of rising higher; menial duties are humble chores; to “perfect herself” is to become more educated and refined. Mrs. Danby speaks in a country way: “peart” means lively, “birogrophy” is her word for biography, and a “billerous attack” is a bilious one, an old name for a sick stomach.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Danbys,” from the opening until Mrs. Danby says good-morning to Mr. Reed; opens “WHO were the Danbys?”; closes “And thus exclaiming to herself, the dear old talker went back into the house.”.

questions.prompt: How are the Reeds and the Danbys different? Where does the narrator say the great contrast ends?
facilitatorNotes: The Reeds are three people with four servants, a mansion, horses and wealth; the Danbys are twelve, with no servants, a little house, one cow and five pigs. The contrast ends with character: the Danbys are respectable, kind and happy.
evidence: the Reeds were a small family of three, with four servants; the Danbys were a large family of twelve, with no servants
There the great contrast ended.

questions.prompt: How did Mr. Danby make his children’s names easier to remember? Why do the last three have only one name?
facilitatorNotes: He named them in alphabetical order and gave each two names, “so as to give them their choice in after life.” After Gregory George, the narrator jokes, the stock of double names gave out. Even so, their mother counts them on her fingers.
evidence: insisted on their being named in alphabetical order
the stock of double names seems to have given out

questions.prompt: Mrs. Danby is sure Amanda Arabella is a genius. How does the narrator hint that her poetry may be less grand than her mother thinks?
facilitatorNotes: Amanda hands her mother the dish-water so that she can write about a rainbow, plans to “perfect herself” without knowing where or how, and stands in the doorway hunting for a rhyme for olives. The narrator is amused, but also fond of her.
evidence: 'Ma!' says she, a-callin' me, 'take this 'ere dish-water!'
she had not the slightest idea of where she could go, and in just what way she was to be perfected

questions.prompt: Mrs. Danby says her children have “more brains than they've a fair right to,” being poor. Does the narrator agree? What do you think of the idea?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says the children are clever and only lack schooling, so being poor has nothing to do with brains. Mrs. Danby’s joke shows that she half believes poor children shouldn’t be so clever. Readers can discuss why someone might think so and what is wrong with it.
evidence: seem to have more brains than they've a fair right to--bein' poor folks' children
they were sharp little things, and native wit served them whenever reading, writing, and arithmetic failed

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: Fandy’s sermon (Chapter VII, second part)
readings.challenge: Enjoy a speech full of mistakes, and work out what the speaker really means.
readings.focus: Eight-year-old Fandy preaches to his brothers and sisters at the pump, and the twins visit Ben.
readings.context: Recap: the Danbys are the Reeds’ poor neighbours, a cheerful family of ten children named in alphabetical order, from Amanda Arabella, who writes poetry, to Baby Jamie. Mrs. Danby, a great talker, has just told Uncle George (Mr. Reed) all about them. Fandy (Francis Ferdinand) is eight; Ben, fifteen, is home after four years of adventures; Gregory is called ’Gory. A boarder pays to live and eat with a family; a roller-towel is shared by everyone; a parson is a minister. Fandy mixes up big words: “extort” is his word for exhort, which means to urge, and “umpressed” for impressed. Ben traps animals for their skins.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Danbys,” from Amanda’s search for a rhyme until Ben asks to borrow Donald’s gun; opens “"Forgot what, Ma?" asked Amanda, who stood in the doorway trying to think of a rhyme for…”; closes “…at a mark in the afternoon, with Uncle and the girls. But we'll use the rifle for that."”.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Danby says of her new boarder, “I don't feel like trustin' him.” Why does she take him anyway? Who might he be?
facilitatorNotes: The family needs the money, and she feels poor folk should not refuse a paying boarder. Many readers will suspect the stranger Uncle George warned the twins about; the chapter does not say.
evidence: I don't feel like trustin' him somehow
it isn't for plain folks to be refusing a real boarder

questions.prompt: What made Fandy climb the step-ladder to preach? What is the main point of his sermon?
facilitatorNotes: The washing-up has turned into splashing, squabbling over the roller-towel and saucy talk. His point is that they should be good and polite and put up with one another, and he admits he cannot manage it alone.
evidence: we all ought to be good and perlite
I can't do it all alone

questions.prompt: Find a place where Fandy breaks off his sermon to scold someone. What does that show about him as a preacher?
facilitatorNotes: He threatens Gregory over Helen’s doll and tells David to stop answering back. The good preacher is not very patient himself, which is funny; he also has sharp eyes, since he spots the twins peeping through the crack.
evidence: Now you, Gregory, give Helen back her dolly right away, or I'll come down to you!
I also can see two people lookin' through the crack

questions.prompt: Fandy says grown-ups “rub our noses the wrong way when they wash our faces.” What is his advice? Is it wise, funny, or both?
facilitatorNotes: Children should be patient until they grow up and have children of their own. It is funny because it turns the usual grown-up lecture round, and a little wise because it asks for patience on both sides.
evidence: It's natural for big folks to rub our noses the wrong way when they wash our faces
An' all we can do is to be patient, an' wait till we get big an' have chil'ren of our own.

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: learn by missing (Chapter VII, end)
readings.challenge: Notice what characters want but do not say aloud.
readings.focus: Ben explains how he shoots without aiming, and Charity Cora tells Dorothy how much she longs to learn.
readings.context: Recap: the twins have walked over to visit the Danbys, their poor, lively neighbours. They overheard eight-year-old Fandy preaching to his brothers and sisters about politeness, then found Ben, the eldest boy, mending a trap. Ben asked to borrow Donald’s gun on Thanksgiving Day. Josie Manning and Ed Tyler are friends of the twins. Dr. Lane, the twins’ tutor, is leaving, and a new teacher is coming. Pungent remarks are sharp ones; a simile compares two things using like or as; the muzzle is the open end of a gun; “punkin” is a country way of saying pumpkin.
readings.contentNote: Ben compares his shooting to the way “an Indian” shoots an arrow, a stereotype of Native Americans common in Dodge’s time. The boys talk about shooting birds and ducks.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Danbys,” from Charity’s question “What girls?” to the end of the chapter; opens “"What girls?" asked Charity Cora, eagerly, hoping, from Donald's plural way of putting…”; closes “…to sit down on a tree-stump, and have a good long talk, if the baby would allow it.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Charity ask “What girls?” How does Dan’s answer make her feel?
facilitatorNotes: She hopes that she and Ella might be invited to the shooting. Dan mocks her with Queen Victoria and the princess, and she feels ashamed. The rich children’s friends are invited; the poor neighbours are not.
evidence: hoping, from Donald's plural way of putting it, that she and Ella Elizabeth possibly were to have a share in the sport
feeling rather ashamed, rubbed her arms

questions.prompt: Explain Ben’s way of shooting a flying bird. Why does Dan want to try “learn by missing” at school, and why does Fandy refuse?
facilitatorNotes: Fire ahead of the bird so that the shot meets it, and get better by practice. Dan jokes that it would excuse his mistakes at school; serious, admiring Fandy will not agree.
evidence: you fire ahead and meet him
Learn by missing.
said the inflexible Fandy

questions.prompt: Charity complains about Baby Jamie, then kisses him “over and over.” What does this show about her feelings?
facilitatorNotes: Caring for him all day is tiring, but she loves him and is proud that he wants her more than the visitor. The complaints and the kisses are both true.
evidence: I tote him round from morning to night--so I do!
looked in placid triumph at Dorothy, apparently forgetting that she ever had made the slightest complaint against him

questions.prompt: What does Charity wish for, and what keeps getting in her way? How might Dorothy feel, hearing it?
facilitatorNotes: She longs for a teacher every day, but housework, the baby and now the boarder keep her from school. Dorothy, who was glad to be rid of algebra and her tutor, might feel lucky, or a little ashamed. Her feelings are not told, so readers must guess.
evidence: I'm just dying to learn things.
There's so much to do in the house

readings.title: Donald and Dorothy: Dorry rides Lady (Chapter VIII)
readings.challenge: Follow a fast action scene, and decide how the chapter title fits it.
readings.focus: Dorothy talks Jack into letting her ride the spirited mare, and the ride turns into a runaway.
readings.context: Recap: the twins have spent the afternoon with the Danbys, their poor, lively neighbours: Ben, fifteen, who has had adventures; Charity Cora, who carries Baby Jamie everywhere; Dan; and little Fandy, eight. Jack, who saved the twins from the shipwreck, is now Uncle George’s coachman and still talks like a sailor. “On her beam ends” means tipped over; a skiff is a small boat; to tauten is to tighten; “Shiver my timbers!” is a sailor’s oath; he calls Uncle George “the Capt’n.” A side-saddle lets a rider in a skirt sit with both legs on one side; the girth is the strap that holds a saddle on; to canter is to run at an easy gallop. “Tandy” in one sentence is Fandy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Too Much of a Good Thing,” the whole chapter; opens “JUST as Donald and Dorothy were about to end the outdoor visit to the Danbys described in…”; closes “…we were in the house. All's right, Jack. Good-by, everybody! We'll skip along home, now."”.

questions.prompt: How does Fandy help catch the mare? Why does he succeed where the man and the big boys failed?
facilitatorNotes: He brings oats in his hat and backs slowly away, shaking them. The chasers only made her run; he gave her a reason to come.
evidence: But what animal is proof against its appetite?
The little midget and his hatful succeeded, where big man and boys had failed.

questions.prompt: Jack says, “No, miss, I won't!” and then saddles the mare. How does Dorry change his mind, and what does he think of himself?
facilitatorNotes: She reminds him that Uncle George said no horse could throw her, and coaxes and hurries him. He calls himself an old fool who can never refuse her anything.
evidence: There isn't a horse on the place that could throw me. Uncle said so.
"I'm an old fool," muttered Jack to himself

questions.prompt: Why does Dorry keep holding on when the ride grows dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: Pride: she feels triumphant because Don and the others are watching, and she will not be beaten in front of “those boys.” Readers can decide whether that was courage or stubbornness.
evidence: Next came a sense of triumph, because she felt that Don and the rest were seeing it all
she certainly could not consent to be conquered before "those boys."

questions.prompt: Donald insists Dot will not be thrown, and at the end calls it “a splendid ride.” Is he being honest? Why does he talk this way?
facilitatorNotes: His face shows that he is frightened, and he rides to the rescue at once. Afterwards he plays it down to protect his sister’s pride and calm everyone. Some readers will call that kind; others may say he is hiding his own fright.
evidence: But his looks betrayed his anxiety.
It's only been a splendid ride for her, and a jolly scare for us
